candidate.answerReason: Bob's counterclockwise move of 9 has the same endpoint as a clockwise move of 3. Alice therefore gains 2 points per turn, first completing a relative circuit of 12 points after 6 turns.

methods.label: Compare their clockwise progress
methods.explanation:
Since only their stopping points matter, replace Bob's move of \(9\) points counterclockwise by the equivalent move of
\[
12-9=3
\]
points clockwise. Both moves end at the same point on this twelve-point circle.

Viewed this way, Alice moves \(5\) points clockwise each turn while Bob moves \(3\), so Alice gains \(2\) points per turn. They start together and stop together again exactly when her accumulated gain is a whole number of twelve-point circuits.

After the first six turns, her gains are
\[
2,\ 4,\ 6,\ 8,\ 10,\ 12.
\]
The first five gains are not complete circuits, while the sixth is exactly one circuit. Thus their first common stopping point after play begins occurs after \(\boxed{6}\) turns, choice A.
methods.levelReason: The circular remainder idea is explained through whole circuits and small integer gains, using only elementary arithmetic.

candidate.annotationRationale: Matching stopping points means that the difference in clockwise step counts is a multiple of 12, exactly the divisibility-of-difference concept in math:modular-congruence. The explanation expresses this through whole circuits. Multiples are the supporting knowledge; greatest common factors are not used.

review.mathematicalCheck: Bob's counterclockwise move of nine has the same endpoint as three clockwise steps. Alice therefore gains two steps per turn. The gains on turns one through six are 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, so the first positive whole relative circuit occurs on turn six.
review.levelCheck: The whole-circuit explanation makes the endpoint condition and exclusion of earlier turns accessible at AMC 8 level.
review.annotationCheck: The difference being a multiple of 12 supports math:modular-congruence conceptually. Multiples are relevant support, and greatest common factors are correctly omitted from the actual method.
